analogy.p: Open source software is like a recipe book shared with everyone: you can see every ingredient and step, change the recipe to suit your taste, and pass your improved version on. Proprietary software is like a sealed ready meal from a restaurant chain: you can eat it as supplied but cannot see the recipe, and you are not allowed to copy the dish and sell it. If it is wrong, you phone the company helpline rather than fixing it yourself. The analogy breaks down because a recipe book is useful only if you can cook, whereas software can be run by anyone, and copying software costs nothing.
analogy.t: A recipe book versus a ready meal

bullets: **Source code**: the human-readable instructions written by programmers.
**Executable / machine code**: the binary version produced by translation, which the computer runs directly.
If you only have the executable, you can run the program but you **cannot easily see or safely change how it works**.
If you have the source code, you can **read, fix, improve and recompile** it.
**Open source** supplies the source code; **proprietary** keeps it secret.
Link to translators: this is why compilers matter, they turn source code into the program users receive.
core.h: Source code versus executable code: the key to the whole topic
core.p: Programmers write **source code** in a high-level language such as Python. A **compiler** or **interpreter** turns it into **machine code (executable code)** that the processor can run. People can read and change source code, but machine code is practically unreadable. The difference between open source and proprietary software is whether the user is given the **source code** or only the **executable**. This single idea explains almost every advantage and disadvantage in exam answers.

bullets: Source code is **publicly available** to download and study.
Users may **modify** the code to suit their own needs, within the licence terms.
Modified versions can usually be **redistributed**, sometimes with the condition that they stay open source.
Often **free to obtain**, though support or extras may be sold.
Developed by **communities of volunteers** and organisations who fix bugs and add features.
Examples: **Linux** (operating system), **LibreOffice** (office suite), **Firefox** (web browser), **GIMP** (image editor), **Python**.
It is still protected by **copyright**; the licence simply gives extra permissions.
core.p: **Open source software** is software whose source code is made freely available so that anyone can **view, modify and redistribute** it, as allowed by its licence. It is usually developed by a **community** of volunteers and sometimes companies, who share improvements publicly. 'Open' refers to the code being open to inspection and change; the software is very often free of charge, but the key idea is freedom to use and adapt it, not just a zero price. Examples you can quote include **Linux, LibreOffice, Mozilla Firefox, GIMP, Python and the Apache web server**.

bullets: Source code is **not available**; only the executable is supplied.
The user receives a **licence**, not ownership; modification and redistribution are not permitted.
Usually **paid for** (one-off purchase or subscription), although some proprietary programs are free to use.
Developed by a **company** with paid professional developers and testers.
Typically comes with **official technical support**, documentation and updates.
Examples: **Windows, Microsoft Office, Adobe Photoshop, macOS**.
Protected by **copyright** and the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
core.p: **Proprietary software** is owned by a company or individual who keeps the **source code secret**. Users buy or license the compiled program and may only use it under the terms of the **End User Licence Agreement (EULA)**. They are not allowed to copy it, modify it or share it. The company is responsible for developing, testing, supporting and updating it, and it makes its money from licence fees or subscriptions. Examples include **Microsoft Windows, Microsoft Office, Adobe Photoshop and many commercial video games**.

bullets: **Free or low cost**: reduces spending and removes the need for large numbers of licences.
**Can be modified** to fit specific needs, for example a school adding features to a learning platform.
**Large community** of developers means bugs may be found and fixed quickly.
**Transparency**: anyone can inspect the code for security flaws or hidden spyware.
**No vendor lock-in**: you are not dependent on one company's decisions or prices.
**Long life**: if the original developers stop, others can continue the project.
**Learning**: students can study real programs' code.
core.p: Open source is attractive because it is usually cheap, flexible and transparent. Because the code is public, users can adapt it for special requirements and many programmers can look for mistakes. This is described as 'many eyes' reviewing the code. For a school or small business with limited money and some technical skill, open source can be a very sensible choice. When writing advantages, always add the reason, not just the label.

bullets: **Limited official support**: help may come from forums rather than a guaranteed helpdesk.
**Variable quality**: some projects are less thoroughly tested or have a less friendly interface.
**Hackers can read the code** to look for vulnerabilities as well as developers.
May need **technical skill** to install, configure or modify.
**Compatibility**: files may not always match those of well-known proprietary programs.
**No guarantee of updates**: a volunteer project may be abandoned.
Poor or missing **documentation** in some projects.
core.p: The same openness creates risks. Support is often less formal and depends on forums and volunteers, so a business with a serious problem may have no one it can contact directly. The software may be less polished or lack some features of paid alternatives, and the quality varies between projects. Because attackers can read the code too, they may find weaknesses, although the community also patches them. Some projects are poorly documented or abandoned.

bullets: **Professional support**: helpdesks, manuals and training from the supplier.
**Rigorous testing** and quality control by paid teams before release.
**Regular updates** and security patches managed by the company.
**Accountability**: the supplier is responsible and may offer a warranty.
Usually a **polished, familiar interface** and wide compatibility with other business software.
**Source code is secret**, which makes it harder for attackers to examine for weaknesses (though not impossible).
Often **integrated** with other products from the same company.
core.p: Proprietary software is usually supported by a company with a reputation to protect. This means professionally tested software, a clear route for help, regular updates and training materials. Businesses often like the predictability and accountability, since there is a named supplier who is responsible if something fails. It is also often better known so staff already know how to use it.

bullets: **Cost**: purchase price or subscription fees, often per user.
**Cannot modify** the software to fit special needs.
**Dependent on the vendor** for fixes and new features (vendor lock-in).
**Licence restrictions** limit how many devices or users can use it.
**Security issues are hidden** from outside review, so users must trust the company.
**Support may end** when a product reaches end of life, forcing upgrades.
Updates may **force changes** or extra costs on users.
core.p: The main drawbacks are cost and lack of control. Licences can be expensive, especially for many users, and the customer cannot change the software or fix a bug themselves. If the company raises prices, stops supporting the product or goes out of business, users have few options. Vendor lock-in is a real concern because file formats and tools may only work with that company's products.

bullets: **Source code**: open source = available; proprietary = secret.
**Cost**: open source = usually free; proprietary = paid licence or subscription.
**Modification**: open source = allowed (within licence); proprietary = not allowed.
**Support**: open source = community/forums; proprietary = official helpdesk and documentation.
**Development**: open source = community collaboration; proprietary = company-employed developers.
**Security**: open source = many people can inspect and fix, but attackers can read it; proprietary = hidden code, but flaws may stay unnoticed.
**Examples**: open source = Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox; proprietary = Windows, MS Office, Photoshop.
core.p: In the exam you often need to compare the two clearly. Always compare on the same criteria: **cost, source code, modification, support, security, quality and examples**. Never write only about one type when the question says 'compare' or 'discuss', and use comparative words such as 'whereas', 'however' and 'in contrast'.

bullets: **Limited budget, technical skills available** -> favours open source.
**Needs guaranteed support and training** -> favours proprietary.
**Needs custom features** -> open source can be modified; proprietary cannot.
**Needs wide compatibility with industry standard files** -> proprietary may be safer.
**Many users** -> licence costs of proprietary rise quickly.
**Security-critical** -> either could work; justify with testing, updates and review.
Always **name the user** and their need in your answer, rather than listing general points.
core.h: Choosing between them: applying to scenarios
core.p: Scenario questions reward answers that match the features of the software to the needs of the user. There is rarely one 'correct' choice, so give a reasoned recommendation using details from the question. A good model: state the choice, give a feature of that software, then link it to the user's situation. For example, a school with a tight budget and a skilled IT team may pick **open source** to save on licence fees and customise it, while a hospital that needs guaranteed support may prefer **proprietary** because of the helpdesk and accountability.

bullets: A licence is **permission with conditions**.
**Proprietary licence**: you may use it, usually on a limited number of devices, but not copy, modify or sell it.
**Open source licence**: permission to view, change and share, often with conditions such as **keeping the licence** and **crediting the authors**.
**Copyleft** (for example the GNU General Public Licence) requires derivative work to remain open.
Using open source code in your own product without following its licence is still **infringement**.
Link: both rely on the **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988**.
core.h: Licences: how copyright links to open source and proprietary software
core.p: Both kinds of software are protected by copyright, and a **licence** says what you are allowed to do. A proprietary licence is restrictive. An open source licence grants extra freedoms, for example to modify and share, and some (known as **copyleft** licences) require that modified versions are also released as open source. Breaking either type of licence is a breach of copyright and could lead to legal action. This links directly to the **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988**.

bullets: Public **repository** holds the code and its history.
Contributors **copy, modify and propose** changes.
**Maintainers review** changes and decide what to release.
A **fork** is a separate copy that goes in a new direction.
Users **report bugs** that volunteers may fix.
Funding may come from **donations, sponsorship or companies** that sell support.
core.h: Open source in practice: how a community project works
core.p: A typical open source project stores its code in a public **repository**. Anyone can download (copy) the code, fix a bug or add a feature, and then submit their change for review. A group of **maintainers** decides which changes to accept and release in the next version. This shared approach spreads the workload, brings in different skills and speeds up bug discovery, but it also means that decisions can be slow or contested and quality depends on the community.

bullets: **Operating systems**: Linux (open) vs Windows/macOS (proprietary).
**Translators**: compilers produce the executable that proprietary vendors distribute.
**Security**: transparency vs obscurity; both need regular updates.
**Legislation**: licences are enforced through copyright law.
**Cost and stakeholders**: choices affect schools, businesses and individuals differently.
**Environmental/sustainability**: open source can keep old hardware useful longer by running lightweight systems.
core.p: This topic joins up with many others. In **systems software**, Linux is an open source operating system while Windows is proprietary. In **translators**, the compiler/interpreter explains why proprietary firms distribute only machine code. In **cybersecurity**, openness versus secrecy affects how vulnerabilities are found. In **ethics and legislation** it links to copyright and to the idea of sharing knowledge freely. Making these links is how you move from a basic to a top-band answer.

exam: 1-mark: define by the key difference: open source = **source code available**; proprietary = **source code not available**.
2-mark describe/compare: give one point about each type, using 'whereas' to show the contrast (for example 'open source allows modification whereas proprietary does not').
Advantages/disadvantages: give the point AND the reason or consequence, for example 'free, so reduces costs for the school'.
For scenario questions, refer to the named user and make a **recommendation** with justification, not a list of generic points.
In 6-mark discuss questions, include both types, advantages and disadvantages, then a conclusion based on the user's needs.
Always use the words **source code**, **licence**, **community**, **support** and **modify**; these match mark scheme wording.
Do not say 'open source is free' without qualification; say 'usually free of charge'.
Give named examples when asked: Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox (open); Windows, Microsoft Office, Photoshop (proprietary).
If asked about security, mention both sides: many people can check open code, but attackers can also read it.
Link to the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act when licences or illegal copying come up.

mistakes.r: Open source means the source code is available and can be modified; it is often free but companies may charge for support or extras.
mistakes.w: Open source software is always free of charge.

mistakes.r: Open code can be checked by many people and fixed quickly, but attackers can also read it; both sides should be stated.
mistakes.w: Open source software is insecure because anyone can see the code.

mistakes.r: Quality varies; proprietary usually has professional support and testing, but open source can be very high quality.
Open source software is still protected by copyright and has a licence with conditions.
mistakes.w: Open source means there are no rules or licences.

mistakes.r: The licence does not permit copying or sharing; this is illegal under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
mistakes.w: I can copy proprietary software if I only use it at home.

mistakes.r: They describe how the software is licensed and whether the source code is available, not what the software does.
mistakes.w: Open source and proprietary describe types of programs like games or word processors.

mistakes.r: They can modify it only within the licence terms, which may require credit and keeping it open.
mistakes.w: Anyone can change open source software and sell it however they like.

mistakes.r: Hidden code is not a guarantee of security; vulnerabilities can still be found and exploited.
mistakes.w: Proprietary software cannot be hacked as the code is hidden.

summary: You must know the difference between open source software (source code available to view, modify and redistribute) and proprietary software (source code kept secret, supplied only as an executable under a licence), and be able to give the advantages and disadvantages of each for a given user. It matters because Paper 1 questions ask you to compare the two and recommend one for a scenario.

terms.d: Software whose source code is freely available to view, modify and redistribute under its licence.
Software owned by a company whose source code is kept secret and which is supplied under a restrictive licence.
The human-readable instructions of a program, written in a programming language.
The machine code version of a program, produced by translation, which the computer can run directly.
A legal agreement that states what a user may and may not do with software.
A translator that converts the whole of the source code into executable machine code.
When a customer depends on one supplier's product and finds it difficult or costly to switch.
A group of volunteers or organisations who develop and support open source software together.
A type of open source licence that requires modified versions to be released under the same open terms.
Help provided to users, such as manuals, helplines and updates.
End User Licence Agreement: the terms the user accepts when installing proprietary software.
A copy of open source software that is developed separately in a new direction.
A change released to fix a bug or security flaw.
Software users are free to use, study, change and share; often, but not always, free of charge.

worked.ans: The charity should use open source software such as LibreOffice and GIMP (1). They are usually free to obtain, so the charity saves money on licences (1), and they can be installed on as many computers as needed (1). A drawback is less official support, but community forums and documentation can help (1).
worked.q: A small charity with a limited budget needs a word processor and image editor. Recommend open source or proprietary software and justify your choice. (4 marks)
steps: Reason 1: free or low cost, so suits limited budget.
Reason 2: can be modified/does not need many licences.
Acknowledge a drawback: limited official support, mitigated by community help.

worked.ans: Open source software makes the source code available whereas proprietary software keeps it secret (1). Open source is usually free whereas proprietary normally requires a paid licence (1). Proprietary software typically has official technical support, whereas open source relies on community forums (1). Users can modify open source code but are not allowed to modify proprietary software (1).
worked.q: Compare open source and proprietary software. (4 marks)

worked.ans: Proprietary software offers a company helpdesk and guaranteed updates, so problems with records can be fixed quickly and the supplier is accountable (2). It is thoroughly tested and the code is not public, which may help protect sensitive data, but it is expensive and the hospital cannot change it (1). Open source is cheaper and can be customised to hospital needs, and many people can inspect the code for weaknesses (2), but support may be less reliable and attackers can read the code (1). Because patient records are critical and sensitive, proprietary software with guaranteed support is probably the better choice, unless the hospital has strong in-house skills (1).
worked.q: A hospital is choosing software for its patient records. Discuss whether it should choose open source or proprietary software. (6 marks)
steps: Proprietary points: professional support, accountability, regular updates, testing.
Open source points: low cost, can be customised, transparency.
Disadvantages of each: cost/vendor lock-in vs less formal support.
